claim: Planar cell polarity (PCP) is the coordinated and consistent orientation of cells in the plane of epithelial sheets.
source: Planar cell polarity (PCP), the coordinated and consistent orientation of cells in the plane of epithelial sheets, is a fundamental and conserved property of animals and plants.
evidence: This is a definitional statement that draws from established scientific consensus about what PCP is.

claim: PCP is a fundamental and conserved property of animals and plants.
source: Planar cell polarity (PCP), the coordinated and consistent orientation of cells in the plane of epithelial sheets, is a fundamental and conserved property of animals and plants.
evidence: This statement reflects established scientific knowledge about the conservation of PCP across kingdoms.

claim: The smallest unit expressing PCP has been considered to be an entire single cell.
source: Up to now, the smallest unit expressing PCP has been considered to be an entire single cell.
evidence: This reflects the prior understanding in the field before the current study.

claim: In the larval epidermis of Drosophila, different subdomains of one cell can have opposite polarities.
source: We report that, in the larval epidermis of Drosophila, different subdomains of one cell can have opposite polarities.
evidence: This is the primary finding of the study, supported by experimental observations shown in figures and quantified in Table 1.

claim: In larvae, PCP is driven by the Dachsous/Fat system.
source: In larvae, PCP is driven by the Dachsous/Fat system
evidence: This is supported by mutant analysis (Figure 3A-D, Table 1) and prior literature on the Ds/Ft system.

claim: The polarity of a subdomain within one cell is its response to levels of Dachsous/Fat in the membranes of contacting cells.
source: we show that the polarity of a subdomain within one cell is its response to levels of Dachsous/Fat in the membranes of contacting cells.
evidence: This is supported by observations of atypical cells and their neighbors (Figures 2, 3, Table 1).

claim: During larval development, cells rearrange.
source: During larval development, cells rearrange (Saavedra et al., 2014)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: When two subdomains of a single cell have different types of neighbouring cells, then these subdomains can become polarised in opposite directions.
source: when two subdomains of a single cell have different types of neighbouring cells, then these subdomains can become polarised in opposite directions.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the atypical cells shown in Figures 2 and quantified in Table 1.

claim: Polarisation depends on a local comparison of the amounts of Dachsous and Fat within opposing regions of a cell's membrane.
source: We conclude that polarisation depends on a local comparison of the amounts of Dachsous and Fat within opposing regions of a cell's membrane.
evidence: This is the main conclusion drawn from the experimental observations of multipolar cells.

claim: At least two genetic systems are involved in PCP and these are conserved between Drosophila and the mouse.
source: At least two genetic systems are involved in PCP and these are conserved between Drosophila and the mouse (Casal et al., 2006; Lawrence et al., 2007; Goodrich and Strutt, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: PCP is envisaged as a cellular property, the smallest unit of manifest polarity being an entire single cell.
source: PCP is envisaged as a cellular property, the smallest unit of manifest polarity being an entire single cell.
evidence: This reflects the prior understanding in the field.

claim: Different domains within a single cell can have mutually opposing polarities in Drosophila.
source: However, we now show in Drosophila that different domains within a single cell can have mutually opposing polarities.
evidence: This is the main finding of the study, supported by experimental data in Figures 2, 3 and Table 1.

claim: Multipolar cells occur in the normal larval epidermis.
source: These multipolar cells occur in the normal larval epidermis
evidence: This is demonstrated by observations in wild-type larvae shown in Figures 1 and 2.

claim: Multipolar cells are detectable because the cells are large and some are decorated with several pointed denticles.
source: These multipolar cells occur in the normal larval epidermis and are detectable because the cells are large and some are decorated with several pointed denticles.
evidence: This is based on direct observation of larval epidermal cells shown in the figures.

claim: The Dachsous/Fat (Ds/Ft) system acts at intercellular contacts.
source: The Dachsous/Fat (Ds/Ft) system acts at intercellular contacts (Strutt and Strutt, 2002; Ma et al., 2003; Casal et al., 2006)
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The polarity of a domain within one cell is its response to the levels of Ds/Ft in neighbouring cells.
source: we provide evidence that the polarity of a domain within one cell is its response to the levels of Ds/Ft in neighbouring cells.
evidence: This is supported by experimental observations of atypical cells and their neighbors.

claim: When another domain of that same responding cell has different neighbours, it can acquire the opposite polarity.
source: When another domain of that same responding cell has different neighbours, it can acquire the opposite polarity.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the multipolar cells shown in Figure 2 and quantified in Table 1.

claim: Polarisation of a domain results from a comparison of the amounts of Ds and Ft in different regions of the cell membrane.
source: We conclude that polarisation of a domain results from a comparison of the amounts of Ds and Ft in different regions of the cell membrane.
evidence: This is the main conclusion inferred from the experimental observations.

claim: The comparison is made between limited regions of membranes on opposite sides of the same cell that face each other along the anterior to posterior axis.
source: This comparison is made between limited regions of membranes on opposite sides of the same cell that face each other along the anterior to posterior axis.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that different subdomains of the same cell can have opposite polarities.

claim: 'Conduits' span across the cell and mediate the comparison of Ds and Ft levels.
source: We conjecture that 'conduits' span across the cell and mediate this comparison.
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis proposed to explain the local comparison mechanism.

claim: The orientation of the conduits, a consequence of the comparison, cues the polarity of denticles.
source: In each region of the cell, the orientation of the conduits, a consequence of the comparison, cues the polarity of denticles.
evidence: This is a speculative mechanism proposed to explain how local comparisons determine denticle orientation.

claim: The epidermis of the later larval stages of Drosophila offers considerable advantages for the analysis of PCP.
source: As we have shown recently (Saavedra et al., 2014), the epidermis of the later larval stages of Drosophila, the second and third stages, offers considerable advantages for the analysis of PCP.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: The development of single individuals can be followed in the larval epidermis.
source: The development of single individuals can be followed and genetic mosaics can be made and studied in vivo (Saavedra et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work describing the methodology.

claim: Genetic mosaics can be made and studied in vivo in the larval epidermis.
source: The development of single individuals can be followed and genetic mosaics can be made and studied in vivo (Saavedra et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work and demonstrated in Figure 3E-H.

claim: The epidermal cells are large (ca 30 µm across in the third stage).
source: The epidermal cells are large (ca 30 µm across in the third stage)
evidence: This is a direct measurement/observation of cell size.

claim: Epidermal cells show their polarity by forming, first, actin-rich predenticles near the cell membrane and then, oriented denticles in the cuticle that they secrete.
source: The epidermal cells are large (ca 30 µm across in the third stage) and show their polarity by forming, first, actin-rich predenticles near the cell membrane and then, oriented denticles in the cuticle that they secrete.
evidence: This is based on direct observation shown in Figures 1 and 2.

claim: There are about seven rows of denticulate cells in each segment.
source: There are about seven rows of denticulate cells in each segment
evidence: This is based on direct observation shown in Figure 1.

claim: Denticle rows 0, 1, and 4 point forwards.
source: denticle rows 0, 1, and 4 point forwards
evidence: This is based on direct observation shown in Figure 1A,B.

claim: Denticle rows 2, 3, 5, and 6 point backwards.
source: rows 2, 3, 5, and 6 point backwards (Figure 1A,B).
evidence: This is based on direct observation shown in Figure 1A,B.

claim: There are two rows of muscle attachments called tendon cells, T1 and T2.
source: There are two rows of muscle attachments called tendon cells, T1 and T2, that lie between rows 1 and 2, and 4 and 5, respectively (Saavedra et al., 2014) (Figure 1).
evidence: This is based on direct observation and supported by citation.

claim: Tendon cells T1 and T2 lie between rows 1 and 2, and 4 and 5, respectively.
source: There are two rows of muscle attachments called tendon cells, T1 and T2, that lie between rows 1 and 2, and 4 and 5, respectively (Saavedra et al., 2014) (Figure 1).
evidence: This is based on direct observation shown in Figure 1 and supported by citation.

claim: As the first stage develops into the second, there are neither cell divisions nor cell deaths.
source: As the first stage develops into the second, there are neither cell divisions nor cell deaths
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: The epidermal cells rearrange during development from first to second stage.
source: As the first stage develops into the second, there are neither cell divisions nor cell deaths; nevertheless, the epidermal cells rearrange and some change their identities (Saavedra et al., 2014)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Some epidermal cells change their identities during development from first to second stage.
source: As the first stage develops into the second, there are neither cell divisions nor cell deaths; nevertheless, the epidermal cells rearrange and some change their identities (Saavedra et al., 2014)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: The tendon cells form denticles in the embryo and early larva but not in the second and third stages.
source: for example, the tendon cells form denticles in the embryo and early larva (Dilks and DiNardo, 2010) but not in the second and third stages
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work and observation.

claim: Some cells change their polarities during development.
source: some cells even change their polarities (Saavedra et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Protein interactions between neighbouring cells are at the core of known PCP systems.
source: Protein interactions between neighbouring cells are at the core of known PCP systems (Goodrich and Strutt, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a review article.

claim: The protocadherins Ds and Ft form heterodimeric bridges between cells.
source: In one of these systems, the protocadherins Ds and Ft form heterodimeric bridges between cells (reviewed in Lawrence et al., 2007; Thomas and Strutt, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to review articles.

claim: The deployment and orientation of Ds-Ft bridges within different parts of a cell membrane depend on the amounts of Ds and Ft activity in neighbouring cells.
source: The deployment and orientation of Ds-Ft bridges within different parts of a cell membrane depend on the amounts of Ds and Ft activity in neighbouring cells.
evidence: This is based on established understanding of the Ds/Ft system from prior literature.

claim: A cell with a low level of Ds presents more Ft (than Ds) on its membrane.
source: For example, a cell with a low level of Ds presents more Ft (than Ds) on its membrane
evidence: This is based on the known mechanism of Ds-Ft interaction.

claim: A cell with low Ds draws more Ds (than Ft) to the abutting membrane of the neighbour.
source: For example, a cell with a low level of Ds presents more Ft (than Ds) on its membrane and this draws more Ds (than Ft) to the abutting membrane of the neighbour
evidence: This is based on the known mechanism of Ds-Ft interaction.

claim: The relative numbers and orientations of heterodimers allow a comparison between a cell's anterior and posterior neighbours.
source: In this way, the relative numbers and orientations of heterodimers allow a comparison between a cell's anterior and posterior neighbours so that it orients its denticles towards the neighbour with the higher Ds, and/or lower Ft, activity (Ma et al., 2003; Casal et al., 2006; Matakatsu and Blair, 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: A cell orients its denticles towards the neighbour with the higher Ds, and/or lower Ft, activity.
source: In this way, the relative numbers and orientations of heterodimers allow a comparison between a cell's anterior and posterior neighbours so that it orients its denticles towards the neighbour with the higher Ds, and/or lower Ft, activity (Ma et al., 2003; Casal et al., 2006; Matakatsu and Blair, 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work and demonstrated in the current study.

claim: The hypothetical model of Ds activity derives from mutant phenotypes of the third stage larvae.
source: This model derives from mutant phenotypes of the third stage larvae (Casal et al., 2006; Donoughe and DiNardo, 2011)
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The model of Ds activity derives from experiments in which the distribution of Ds was manipulated at later stages.
source: This model derives from mutant phenotypes of the third stage larvae (Casal et al., 2006; Donoughe and DiNardo, 2011) and experiments in which the distribution of Ds was manipulated, also at later stages (Repiso et al., 2010; Donoughe and DiNardo, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The model depends on the pattern of expression of four-jointed (Fj), a kinase that activates Ft and deactivates Ds.
source: The model also depends on the pattern of expression of four-jointed (Fj), a kinase that activates Ft and deactivates Ds (Brittle et al., 2010; Simon et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: fj is much more strongly expressed in the tendon cells than elsewhere.
source: fj is much more strongly expressed in the tendon cells than elsewhere—it should lower the activity of Ds in these cells—and graded in cells from rows 2 (high) to 4 (low) (Saavedra et al., in preparation).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to work in preparation.

claim: fj expression should lower the activity of Ds in tendon cells.
source: fj is much more strongly expressed in the tendon cells than elsewhere—it should lower the activity of Ds in these cells
evidence: This is inferred from the known function of Fj.

claim: fj is graded in cells from rows 2 (high) to 4 (low).
source: fj is much more strongly expressed in the tendon cells than elsewhere—it should lower the activity of Ds in these cells—and graded in cells from rows 2 (high) to 4 (low) (Saavedra et al., in preparation).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to work in preparation.

claim: The hypothetical landscape of Ds activity can explain the orientation of all the denticle rows.
source: The hypothetical landscape can explain the orientation of all the denticle rows.
evidence: This is demonstrated by comparing the model in Figure 1C with the observed denticle orientations in Figure 1A,B.

claim: A few row 4 cells are tilted from the mediolateral axis and take up 'atypical' positions.
source: Consider the cells of row 4. A few of these cells are tilted from the mediolateral axis; they take up 'atypical' positions, contributing to two different rows of cells in the normal stack (one is shown in Figure 2A,B, shaded magenta and Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on direct observation shown in Figure 2.

claim: Atypical row 4 cells contribute to two different rows of cells in the normal stack.
source: A few of these cells are tilted from the mediolateral axis; they take up 'atypical' positions, contributing to two different rows of cells in the normal stack (one is shown in Figure 2A,B, shaded magenta and Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on direct observation shown in Figure 2.

claim: One portion of an atypical row 4 cell has denticles that point forwards towards the neighbouring row 3 cell.
source: Thus, this portion of the atypical cell has neighbours exactly like an ideal row 4 cell and its denticles point forwards towards the neighbouring row 3 cell (Figure 2A–D and Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on direct observation shown in Figure 2.

claim: Another portion of the same atypical row 4 cell has denticles that point backwards.
source: However, the other portion of the same atypical cell intervenes between a row 3 and a normal row 4 cell and the denticles in that portion point backwards
evidence: This is based on direct observation shown in Figure 2.

claim: The backwards-pointing polarity adopted by a domain of the atypical cell does not affect the polarity of neighbouring cells.
source: Note that the backwards-pointing polarity adopted by this domain of the atypical cell does not, and is not expected to, affect the polarity of neighbouring cells.
evidence: This is based on observation and inference from the model.

claim: The orientation of denticles in one part of an atypical cell correlates with the anterior and posterior neighbours of that part.
source: To quantitate, we selected atypical cells for study and then ask does the orientation of denticles in one part of a cell correlate with the anterior and posterior neighbours of that part? The answer is very clearly yes (Table 1).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data in Table 1.

claim: A portion of the membrane of one cell can compare itself with that in a facing portion of the same cell and this comparison polarises that particular domain of the cell.
source: these multipolar cells tell us that a portion of the membrane of one cell can compare itself with that in a facing portion of the same cell and this comparison polarises that particular domain of the cell.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation of multipolar cells.

claim: A cell reads the Ds activities of its anterior and posterior neighbours and responds accordingly.
source: By this means a cell reads the Ds activities of its anterior and posterior neighbours and responds accordingly.
evidence: This is inferred from the observations of atypical cells and their denticle orientations.

claim: Atypical cells occur in row 2.
source: Atypical cells occur in other regions of the segment, for example in row 2.
evidence: This is based on direct observation shown in Figure 2E-H.

claim: All predenticles and denticles in atypical row 2 cells point backwards as they do in the wild type.
source: These cells have a mix of neighbours also, and anatomically are equivalent to the atypical cells near row 4; however, all their predenticles and denticles point backwards as they do in the wild type (Figure 2E–H and Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on direct observation shown in Figure 2 and quantified in Table 1.

claim: Atypical cells occur in row 3.
source: Atypical cells also occur in row 3
evidence: This is stated in the text based on observation.

claim: Atypical row 3 cells have portions inserted between a different row 3 and a row 4 cell and their denticles point backwards toward the neighbour cell with higher Ds activity.
source: Atypical cells also occur in row 3; these cells have portions inserted between a different row 3 and a row 4 cell and their denticles point backwards toward the neighbour cell with higher Ds activity, that is row 4 (not shown).
evidence: This is based on observation.

claim: In ds−ft− larvae, atypical cells occur both in rows 2 and 4 and are anatomically similar to those in wild type.
source: Using ds−ft− larvae, we found that atypical cells do occur both in rows 2 and 4 and are anatomically similar to those in wild type.
evidence: This is based on direct observation shown in Figure 3A-D.

claim: The orientation of denticles in atypical cells in ds−ft− larvae is equally indeterminate in both rows and is independent of neighbours.
source: However, the orientation of denticles in these cells is equally indeterminate in both rows and is independent of neighbours (Figure 3A–D, Table 1).
evidence: This is based on direct observation shown in Figure 3A-D and quantified in Table 1.

claim: Without the Ds-Ft intercellular bridges, a cell cannot compare neighbours to ascertain where to point its denticles.
source: This is presumably and simply because, without the Ds-Ft intercellular bridges, a cell cannot compare neighbours to ascertain where to point its denticles.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that ds−ft− mutants show random denticle orientation.

claim: There is no other PCP agent, apart from the Ds/Ft system, that is responsible for multipolar cells in the larva.
source: It also argues that there is no other PCP agent, apart from the Ds/Ft system, that is responsible for these multipolar cells in the larva.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that ds−ft− mutants show random denticle orientation in atypical cells.

claim: Small clones of marked cells that over-express ds were made and studied in the larva in vivo.
source: In a further test, we made small clones of marked cells that over-express ds and studied them in the larva in vivo.
evidence: This is based on the experimental procedure described and shown in Figure 3E-H.

claim: Clones over-expressing ds were initiated early in embryogenesis, around the blastoderm stage and are small, ranging in size from 1 to 5 cells.
source: These clones were initiated early in embryogenesis, around the blastoderm stage and are small, ranging in size from 1 to 5 cells (Saavedra et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Clones over-expressing ds probably begin to make excess Ds in the embryo following the first one or two divisions that occur in the postblastoderm epidermis.
source: They probably begin to make excess Ds in the embryo following the first one or two divisions that occur in the postblastoderm epidermis (Foe and Alberts, 1983; Hartenstein and Campos-Ortega, 1985)
evidence: This is inferred from the timing of clone induction and supported by citations about embryonic development.

claim: Neighbouring wild type cells of clones expressing high levels of ds become repolarised so that their denticles point towards cells with excess Ds.
source: Consistent with observations on the adult of clones expressing high levels of ds (Casal et al., 2002), or on larvae when groups of cells over-express ds (Repiso et al., 2010; Donoughe and DiNardo, 2011), neighbouring wild type cells become repolarised so that their denticles point towards cells with excess Ds.
evidence: This is based on observation shown in Figure 3E-H and supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Portions of cells are affected by ds-expressing clones and the orientation of denticles in that part of the cell in contact with the ds-expressing cell can point inwards whilst other parts of the same cell point in various directions.
source: In larvae, we now find that portions of cells are affected and the orientation of denticles in that part of the cell in contact with the ds-expressing cell can point inwards whilst other parts of the same cell, whose neighbours are not over-expressing ds, point in various directions.
evidence: This is based on direct observation shown in Figure 3E-H.

claim: Multipolar cells induced by ds-expressing clones occasionally affect the polarity of their neighbouring cells.
source: In this and other examples, multipolar cells also appear occasionally to affect the polarity of their neighbouring cells (see legend, Figure 3).
evidence: This is based on observation shown in Figure 3E-H.

claim: Propagation of polarity from multipolar cells seems to be limited to those portions of neighbouring cells that contact regions of the multipolar cells that show an abnormal polarity.
source: However, such a propagation of polarity seems to be limited to those portions of neighbouring cells that contact regions of the multipolar cells that show an abnormal polarity.
evidence: This is inferred from observations of ds-expressing clones.

claim: This local propagation of polarity does not affect row 4 cells.
source: Note however that this local propagation of polarity does not affect row 4 cells.
evidence: This is based on observation.

claim: The low Ds activity of the T2 cells strongly influences the polarity of row 4 cells, strongly enough to counteract any effect that might originate from any multipolar or repolarised row 3 neighbours.
source: We believe that this observation can be explained if the low Ds activity of the T2 cells were to strongly influence the polarity of row 4 cells, strongly enough to counteract any effect that might originate from any multipolar or repolarised row 3 neighbours.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the observation.

claim: The marked ds-expressing cells themselves show no preferred polarity, their denticles pointing in diverse directions.
source: Note that the marked ds-expressing cells themselves show no preferred polarity, their denticles pointing in diverse directions.
evidence: This is based on direct observation shown in Figure 3E-H.

claim: The lack of preferred polarity in ds-expressing cells might be explained by the amount of Ds activity in such cells being much higher than all their neighbours, giving insufficient directional bias to fix their own polarities.
source: This might be explained by the amount of Ds activity in such cells being much higher than all their neighbours, giving insufficient directional bias to fix their own polarities.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the observation.

claim: Gaps in the tendon cell rows often affect the orientation and pattern of denticles, as well as forming some multipolar cells.
source: Such gaps often affect the orientation and pattern of denticles, as well as forming some multipolar cells.
evidence: This is based on observation shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: A cell located next to a gap in the T1 tendon row and thus adjacent to a row 1 and a row 3 cell develops no defined polarity.
source: Consider first a cell that is located next to a gap in the T1 tendon row and thus adjacent to a row 1 and a row 3 cell. The rows 1 and 3 have similar amounts of Ds activity and so the cell in question develops no defined polarity (magenta in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B–D).
evidence: This is based on observation shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1 and inference from the model.

claim: Rows 1 and 3 have similar amounts of Ds activity.
source: The rows 1 and 3 have similar amounts of Ds activity
evidence: This is inferred from the model shown in Figure 1C.

claim: When the T2 row of tendon cells is interrupted, a denticulate cell can come to lie between a row 4 and a row 6 cell.
source: In another case, we see the T2 row of tendon cells is interrupted and in the breach there is a denticulate cell that comes to lie between a row 4 and a row 6 cell (Figure 3—figure supplement 1E–H).
evidence: This is based on direct observation shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: A cell between row 4 and row 6 cells has predenticles and denticles that are placed in the middle of the cell and point in mixed directions.
source: This creates an ambiguous situation as both these neighbours have similar amounts of Ds and give no directional cue. Consequently, the cell in question has predenticles and denticles that are placed in the middle of the cell (Figure 3—figure supplement 1E), giving rise to denticles that are spread over the apical surface of the cell and point in mixed directions (shown in magenta in Figure 2—figure supplement 1F–H).
evidence: This is based on direct observation shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Both row 4 and row 6 neighbours have similar amounts of Ds and give no directional cue.
source: This creates an ambiguous situation as both these neighbours have similar amounts of Ds and give no directional cue.
evidence: This is inferred from the model shown in Figure 1C.

claim: These results offer evidence that the earlier models of the Ds/Ft system apply to these large larval cells, just as they do to the eye, the wing, and the abdomen.
source: These results offer evidence that the earlier models of the Ds/Ft system (Strutt and Strutt, 2002; Casal et al., 2006) apply to these large larval cells, just as they do to the eye (Strutt and Strutt, 2002; Simon, 2004), the wing (Ma et al., 2003), and the abdomen, (Casal et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data and citations to prior work.

claim: The cell membrane of a clone containing excessive amounts of Ds will attract Ft to the abutting membranes of neighbouring cells.
source: For example, in all these organs and stages, the cell membrane of a clone containing excessive amounts of Ds will attract Ft to the abutting membranes of neighbouring cells and lead to a redistribution of Ds-Ft heterodimers in those cells, and even beyond (reviewed in Thomas and Strutt, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by observation in Figure 3E-H and citations to prior work.

claim: Excessive Ds in a clone leads to a redistribution of Ds-Ft heterodimers in neighbouring cells, and even beyond.
source: For example, in all these organs and stages, the cell membrane of a clone containing excessive amounts of Ds will attract Ft to the abutting membranes of neighbouring cells and lead to a redistribution of Ds-Ft heterodimers in those cells, and even beyond (reviewed in Thomas and Strutt, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by observation and citations to prior work.

claim: The polarity of a cell is the outcome of a comparison between its anterior and posterior membranes.
source: We proposed (Casal et al., 2006) that the polarity of a cell is the outcome of a comparison between its anterior and posterior membranes
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed in prior work and supported by the current observations.

claim: The amount and orientations of Ds-Ft heterodimers are compared and the denticles point towards that region of the cell membrane that has most Ft.
source: We proposed (Casal et al., 2006) that the polarity of a cell is the outcome of a comparison between its anterior and posterior membranes; that the amount and orientations of Ds-Ft heterodimers are compared and the denticles point towards that region of the cell membrane that has most Ft (i.e., abutting a neighbouring cell that has higher Ds levels).
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed in prior work and supported by the current observations.

claim: The multipolar cells provide new evidence for the hypothesis that polarity results from a comparison between anterior and posterior membranes.
source: The multipolar cells provide new evidence for this hypothesis.
evidence: This is based on the observations of multipolar cells in Figures 2 and 3.

claim: The level of Ds in a row 3 cell should be higher than the level of Ds in a T2 cell but lower than the level of Ds in a row 4 cell.
source: First, note that the level of Ds in a row 3 cell should be higher than the level of Ds in a T2 cell but lower than the level of Ds in a row 4 cell (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is inferred from the model shown in Figure 1C.

claim: There is a comparison between the anterior and posterior membranes of the row 4 multipolar cell.
source: Then, consider the following arguments: one that there is a comparison between the anterior and posterior membranes of the row 4 multipolar cell filled in magenta in Figure 2B–C.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation of opposite polarities in different regions of the cell.

claim: The comparison between anterior and posterior membranes is local to different regions of the row 4 multipolar cell.
source: Two, that this comparison is local to different regions of that cell.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that different regions of the same cell have opposite polarities.

claim: Across the whole stretch of its anterior membrane, the row 4 multipolar cell contacts two cells of row 3, each presenting equal amounts of Ds.
source: Across the whole stretch of its anterior membrane this row 4 multipolar cell contacts two cells of row 3, each presenting equal amounts of Ds.
evidence: This is based on observation shown in Figure 2.

claim: Within the posterior membrane of the row 4 multipolar cell there are two separate regions, each abutting cells with different levels of Ds.
source: However, within the posterior membrane of this same multipolar cell there are two separate regions, each abutting cells with different levels of Ds: a region abutting the T2 neighbour, and a region abutting the normal row 4 cell.
evidence: This is based on observation shown in Figure 2.

claim: The region of the multipolar cell abutting the T2 has a lower amount of Ft and a higher amount of Ds than the facing anterior membrane of the same cell, so its denticles point forwards.
source: The region abutting the T2 has a lower amount of Ft (as a result of the low amount of Ds in the T2 cell), and a higher amount of Ds (as a result of the high amount of Ft in the T2 cell) than the facing anterior membrane of the same cell, so its denticles point forwards.
evidence: This is inferred from the model and the observation of denticle orientation.

claim: The region of the multipolar cell abutting the normal row 4 cell has a higher amount of Ft and a lower amount of Ds than in the facing anterior membrane of the same cell, so its denticles point backwards.
source: The region abutting the normal row 4 cell has a higher amount of Ft (as a result of the high amount of Ds in the normal row 4 cell) and a lower amount of Ds (as a result of the lower amount of Ft in the normal row 4 cell) than in the facing anterior membrane of the same cell, so its denticles point backwards.
evidence: This is inferred from the model and the observation of denticle orientation.

claim: Multipolarity tells us that the comparison is local to different regions of the cell.
source: Multipolarity tells us something new and unexpected: that the comparison is local to different regions of the cell.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation of multipolar cells.

claim: The two domains of the multipolar cell are comparing their facing anterior and posterior membranes, independent of each other.
source: The two domains described above are comparing their facing anterior and posterior membranes, independent of each other.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that the two domains have opposite polarities.

claim: The comparison cannot be a signal that pervades the whole cell.
source: Therefore, the comparison cannot be a signal that pervades the whole cell
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that different regions of the same cell have opposite polarities.

claim: Multipolarity suggests the existence of oriented 'conduits' that link facing regions within the anterior and posterior membranes of a single cell.
source: and instead multipolarity suggests the existence of oriented 'conduits' that link facing regions within the anterior and posterior membranes of a single cell.
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis proposed to explain the local comparison mechanism.

claim: If the orientation of conduits were determined by the distribution of Ds and Ft, and if they also helped convey Ds and Ft across the cell, then together both these properties could constitute a feedback mechanism.
source: If such oriented conduits exist they could allow the directional transport and/or unequal stabilisation of components of the polarity machinery (such as Ds and Ft themselves). Our conception of these conduits is yet incomplete; but if their orientation were determined by the distribution of Ds and Ft, and if they also helped convey Ds and Ft across the cell, then together both these properties could constitute a feedback mechanism.
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis about the mechanism of polarity.

claim: Such a feedback mechanism would make the polarity of cells more robust and also would affect the propagation of polarity from cell to cell.
source: Such a mechanism would make the polarity of cells more robust and also would affect the propagation of polarity from cell to cell.
evidence: This is a speculative prediction about the consequences of the proposed mechanism.

claim: The distribution of Ds and Ft within the membrane of one cell is partly determined by the distribution of these molecules in that cell's neighbours and also in cells beyond.
source: Understanding propagation is important because experiments suggest that the distribution of Ds and Ft within the membrane of one cell is partly determined by the distribution of these molecules in that cell's neighbours and also in cells beyond (reviewed in Thomas and Strutt, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a review article.

claim: There is no need to invoke free diffusion of Ds and Ft molecules if they are transported across the cell between limited domains.
source: Note that if Ds and Ft are transported across the cell between limited domains, there is no need to invoke free diffusion of these molecules (as in Mani et al., 2013; Abley et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the mechanism, contrasting with other models.

claim: Similar conduits would be present in all cells, but normally, since they signal consistently in all parts of the cell, they would not be detected as separable elements.
source: Similar conduits would be present in all cells, but normally, since they signal consistently in all parts of the cell, they would not be detected as separable elements.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for why conduits have not been observed in normal cells.

claim: Several authors described oriented microtubules in planar polarised cells.
source: There are hints at what these conduits might be: several authors described oriented microtubules in planar polarised cells (Fristrom and Fristrom, 1975; Eaton et al., 1996; Turner and Adler, 1998)

claim: Microtubule growth and polarity have been studied in the developing wing.
source: several authors described oriented microtubules in planar polarised cells (Fristrom and Fristrom, 1975; Eaton et al., 1996; Turner and Adler, 1998) and studied microtubule growth and polarity in the developing wing (Harumoto et al., 2010; Olofsson et al., 2014).

claim: In a particular part of the wing, and for a relatively short time, there are microtubules that are oriented proximodistally.

source: In any case, a net orientation of microtubules might be read out as a net transport of vesicles from proximal to distal (Shimada et al., 2006; Harumoto et al., 2010; Gault et al., 2012).
